ana_01.label: Post-COVID expedition rebound, 22 to 279 in two years
ana_01.content: Annual expedition counts in the dataset show the COVID-19 collapse and recovery: only 22 expeditions in 2020 (the pandemic year), then 207 in 2021, 279 in 2022 (a 12.7x rebound from 2020), 274 in 2023, and 100 in 2024 (the 2024 figure is partial because the slice was filtered before the autumn 2024 season closed). The 2022 peak coincides with Nepal fully reopening high mountains to foreign climbers and matches the broader media narrative of a record post-pandemic boom that culminated in the 2023 Everest crowding crisis.

ana_02.label: Three peaks absorb half of all expeditions
ana_02.content: Of the 480 catalogued peaks in the Nepal Himalaya, just three accounted for 49.0% of all 2020-2024 expeditions: Everest (189, 21.4%), Ama Dablam (147, 16.7%) and Manaslu (96, 10.9%). The next tier - Lhotse (79), Himlung Himal (51), Dhaulagiri I (35), Makalu (26), Baruntse (24), Annapurna I (22), Kangchenjunga (20) - confirms that climbing tourism is dominated by a small set of marquee peaks. Ama Dablam at 6,812 m is famous for being a 'high altitude trophy' with technical climbing but a lower oxygen-debt; Everest, Manaslu and Lhotse are 8000ers commercialised with fixed-rope highways.

ana_03.label: Success rate by peak: from 93% to 27%
ana_03.content: Among peaks attempted at least 10 times, success rates (TERMREASON in 1, 2 or 3) span an enormous range: Ama Dablam tops the list at 93.2% (137/147), followed by Everest at 89.4% (169/189), Annapurna I at 86.4% (19/22), and Lhotse at 86.1% (68/79). At the bottom, Pumori succeeds only 27.3% of the time (3/11) and Baruntse 33.3% (8/24). Dhaulagiri I, the seventh-highest mountain in the world and not yet equipped with the Everest-grade fixed-rope infrastructure, lies in the middle at 51.4% (18/35). The top of the list is dominated by peaks with paid Sherpa rope-fixing teams.

ana_04.label: Termination reason mix: 71% success, 9% bad weather
ana_04.content: Combining all three success codes (main peak, subpeak, claimed), 74.1% of all 2020-2024 expeditions ended successfully (628 main peak + 26 subpeak = 654 of 882). The single largest failure reason is 'Bad weather (storms, high winds)' at 78 expeditions (8.84%), followed by 'Bad conditions (deep snow, avalanching, falling ice or rock)' at 54 (6.12%) and 'Illness, AMS, exhaustion or frostbite' at 25 (2.83%). Pure technical failure - 'Route technically too difficult, lack of experience, strength or motivation' - is rare at 9 expeditions (1.02%), and accident-driven termination is rarer still at 5 expeditions (0.57%).

ana_05.label: Among failures, weather is king (34%); technical difficulty is marginal (4%)
ana_05.content: Restricting to the 228 expeditions that did NOT succeed, the failure mix shifts dramatically: bad weather alone explains 34.2% of failures (78/228), and bad conditions another 23.7% (54/228). Together, weather and conditions account for 57.9% of expedition failures. Pure technical difficulty - the romantic image of climbers turned back by an unclimbable cliff - explains just 3.95% of failures (9/228). Illness/AMS/frostbite explains 11.0% (25/228), and outright accidents 2.2% (5/228). The picture is dominated by environmental hindrances rather than individual climbing limits, an important framing for the modern, commercially-supported era.

ana_06.label: Oxygen lifts success rate by 38 percentage points
ana_06.content: Of 882 expeditions, 409 used bottled oxygen and 473 did not. Oxygen-using expeditions succeeded 94.4% of the time (386/409) versus 56.7% (268/473) for no-oxygen expeditions - a 37.7 percentage-point gap. Bottled oxygen, in this slice, is the single strongest predictor of summit success of any binary variable in the dataset. The mechanism is straightforward (det_06): above 7,500 m the body cannot acclimatize indefinitely and oxygen lowers the effective altitude, restoring cognition and stamina. This figure echoes the Everest mortality drop attributed to obligatory oxygen for guides.

ana_07.label: Oxygen-using expeditions are 5x more likely to record a death
ana_07.content: Counter-intuitively, oxygen-using expeditions are MORE likely to record at least one death than no-oxygen expeditions: 7.6% (31 of 409) vs 1.5% (7 of 473). This is not because oxygen is unsafe; it is selection bias - oxygen is mainly used on the eight-thousanders (Everest, Manaslu, Lhotse, Cho Oyu) where altitude itself is lethal, while the no-oxygen group skews towards lower trekking peaks like Ama Dablam (6,812 m). Total deaths recorded on O2-using expeditions: 44 (member+hired); without O2: 9. The lesson is that oxygen is the marker of high-altitude commercial climbing, where the danger is the mountain, not the oxygen.

ana_08.label: No-hired expeditions: 30 points lower success, far smaller scale
ana_08.content: Expeditions with NO hired personnel above base camp (the alpine-style purist mode) had a 48.6% success rate (n=146), compared with 79.2% for expeditions that employed hired staff (n=736). They also operated at a much smaller scale: 519 total members across 146 expeditions (~3.6 per team) versus 6,707 members and 6,712 hired across 736 expeditions (~9.1 members + 9.1 hired per team). Member deaths in no-hired teams: 5 of 519 climbers; in hired teams: 31 of 6,707. Per-climber member death rates therefore look comparable, but the no-hired teams achieved their successes with one-tenth the support, and on a different mix of peaks.

ana_09.label: Sherpas are 32% of recorded deaths but earn the same death rate per person
ana_09.content: Across 2020-2024, the dataset records 36 member deaths and 17 hired-staff (Sherpa and other) deaths, for 53 total. Hired staff make up 32.1% of all recorded deaths despite being roughly 48% of the people on the mountain (6,716 hired vs 7,226 members). Per-person death rates: members 4.98 per 1,000, hired 2.53 per 1,000. The gap reflects two things: clients without Sherpa-level acclimatisation are statistically more vulnerable, and Sherpas often turn back with clients before fatal exposure. The figure also disguises the fact that almost all hired deaths cluster around Everest where the icefall and crowding hit Sherpas disproportionately.

ana_10.label: Spring (52%) and Autumn (45%) own the calendar; Winter is brutal
ana_10.content: Seasonality is bimodal. Spring (Mar-May) hosts 52.4% of expeditions (462), Autumn (Sep-Nov) 44.7% (394), Summer just 0.6% (5) and Winter 2.4% (21). Success rates are 77.1% in Spring, 72.8% in Autumn, 60.0% in Summer (n only 5), and a stark 38.1% in Winter. Spring's combination of pre-monsoon stable weather, established rope-fixing, and the famous May summit window keeps it on top; Winter's collapse to 38% reflects unforgiving Himalayan winter weather even when expeditions still attempt it.

ana_11.label: Eight-thousanders: 55% of all expeditions, wildly different death rates
ana_11.content: The eight 8000ers in the Nepal Himalaya absorbed 483 of 882 expeditions (54.8%) in 2020-2024. The death rate per 1,000 people-on-mountain ranges from 0.0 (Cho Oyu, n=212 climbers, 0 deaths) up to 7.30 on Everest (4,659 climbers, 34 deaths) and 6.08 on Kangchenjunga (329 climbers, 2 deaths). Success rates also span widely: from 89.4% on Everest and 86.4% on Annapurna I (n=22 expeditions only, much smaller than the cumulative 13.4% Annapurna fatality rate quoted by Guinness in det_04) down to 51.4% on Dhaulagiri I and 62.5% on Cho Oyu. This slice is too small to overturn the long-run reputation of any peak; it's a snapshot of recent traffic, not history.

ana_13.label: Disputed claims are vanishingly rare in the modern record
ana_13.content: Hawley built her reputation on cross-checking claimed summits. In the 2020-2024 slice, the CLAIMED flag is FALSE on every recorded row (zero rows have CLAIMED=TRUE), while DISPUTED is TRUE on just 2 expeditions. In the modern era of GPS, smartphones, and dense Sherpa eyewitnesses, the room for false summit claims has almost vanished compared to Hawley's heyday in the 1980s and 90s. The detective heritage continues, but the Sherlock Holmes role has shifted from interrogator to record-keeper.

ana_14.label: Camps and rope: 8000ers need 2.2x more camps and 2.7x more rope
ana_14.content: Eight-thousander expeditions average 3.36 high camps above base camp and 27 m of fixed rope per expedition recorded in the dataset; sub-8000 m expeditions average 1.51 camps and 10 m of recorded rope. The infrastructure gap is the visible signature of commercial high-altitude climbing: more camps mean more porter rotations, more oxygen caches, more weather-windows. The rope figures are likely under-reported in the dataset (much commercial rope-fixing is shared between expeditions), but the ratio holds.

ana_15.label: 112 of 480 listed peaks remain unclimbed
ana_15.content: The peaks_tidy table catalogues 480 peaks: 368 marked Climbed and 112 marked Unclimbed (PSTATUS_FACTOR). Unclimbed peaks span 5,407 to 8,077 m with a median of 6,452 m - meaning that even after a century of expeditions, mountains taller than 8,000 m may still appear on the unclimbed list. The Kanti/Palchung range holds the most unclimbed peaks (14), followed by Janak/Ohmi Kangri (12), Api/Byas Risi/Guras (11), Khumbu (11) and Kangchenjunga/Simhalila (9). For climbers seeking first ascents, the western Himalaya and the Janak region remain the frontier.

ana_16.label: 2024 was the best success year (81%); 2023 was second (81%)
ana_16.content: Year-over-year success rates: 2020 77.3% (n=22), 2021 70.0% (n=207), 2022 68.1% (n=279), 2023 80.7% (n=274), 2024 81.0% (n=100, partial). The dip in 2021-2022 is consistent with a rush of less-experienced climbers returning after the pandemic and bidding for a limited weather window; the 2023-2024 recovery suggests the commercial industry recalibrated. The same 2023 season was the deadliest in Everest history (det_03), so high success rates and high deaths can co-exist when sheer volume rises.

data_table.description: Expeditions and success rate by year

caveats.content: The exped_tidy table is filtered to YEAR 2020-2024. 2024 has only 100 rows, almost certainly a partial year captured before the autumn 2024 season closed. Treat 2024 trend lines as preliminary.

TOTDAYS and SMTDAYS contain large numbers of zeros that appear to be missing-value sentinels rather than 'expeditions of zero days'. Mean total-days statistics in this slice should not be quoted; medians come out at 0 and skew the result.

All success/death rates are within-slice rates over 2020-2024 only. Long-run cumulative rates (e.g., Annapurna I 13.4% fatality) belong to det_04 - they are NOT visible in this slice's 22 Annapurna I expeditions and 1 death.

Selection bias warning for the oxygen-vs-deaths finding (ana_07): oxygen use is strongly confounded with peak choice. Oxygen-using expeditions go to 8000ers; no-oxygen expeditions skew towards Ama Dablam and other lower peaks. The death-rate gap reflects altitude, not oxygen.
ROPE column in the dataset has many missing values; recorded averages (ana_14) likely under-count actual fixed rope, especially on Everest and Manaslu where rope-fixing is shared across expeditions.
